lead: A thin plate loaded in its own plane can suddenly bend out of plane when the compressive force reaches a critical value. Its bending stiffness D resists the bending, and the in-plane force, tilted by the bending, feeds it. Equating the two gives the plate buckling equation, an eigenvalue problem whose lowest root is the buckling load. Skin between stringers and ribs, spar webs and the flanges of stringers all buckle this way, and the result sets stringer pitch and skin thickness.
prereq: You need: the plate equation with in-plane forces from plates under transverse and in-plane loads, and Euler column buckling.

sections.h3: The governing equation for plate buckling

blocks.text: Start from the plate equation with in-plane forces and set the pressure to zero. A flat plate under in-plane load is in equilibrium for any load. Buckling asks a different question: at what load can a slightly bent shape also be in equilibrium? Then the plate can move sideways with no lateral load at all. For compression it is convenient to work with positive numbers, so here N<sub>x</sub>, N<sub>y</sub> and N<sub>xy</sub> are taken positive in compression, which reverses the signs of the previous chapter:

blocks.where: w is the buckling deflection (m), small compared with t; D = Et³/[12(1 − ν²)] the plate stiffness (N·m); N<sub>x</sub>, N<sub>y</sub> the in-plane direct forces per unit length (N/m), positive in compression; N<sub>xy</sub> the in-plane shear force per unit length (N/m).

blocks.text: The plate is taken as flat, isotropic, of uniform thickness and elastic. The equation is linear and has no load term, so w = 0 is always a solution. A non-zero shape exists only at particular loads, the eigenvalues; the smallest is the critical load. This sudden change from a flat equilibrium to a bent one at a fixed load is bifurcation, the plate form of structural instability. Tension enters with the opposite sign and raises the buckling load.

Take a plate a × b, length a along the load, simply supported on all four edges, with N<sub>x</sub> only. The edges cannot deflect and carry no moment, so w and its second derivative normal to each edge are zero. The shape w = A sin(mπx/a) sin(nπy/b) meets all of these, with m half-waves along the load and n across. Substituting, each fourth derivative brings out a factor (mπ/a)⁴ and so on, and the equation becomes A × [Dπ⁴(m²/a² + n²/b²)² − N<sub>x</sub> π²m²/a²] = 0. For A ≠ 0:

blocks.where: N<sub>x</sub> is the compressive force per unit length (N/m) at which the (m, n) shape is in equilibrium; a and b are the plate sides (m).

blocks.text: Any n > 1 only raises N<sub>x</sub>, so the plate buckles with one half-wave across, n = 1. Writing r = a/b, the result takes the standard form:
N<sub>cr</sub> = kπ²D/b²,   σ<sub>cr</sub> = kπ²E/[12(1 − ν²)] (t/b)²,   k = (m/r + r/m)²
blocks.where: N<sub>cr</sub> is the critical force per unit length (N/m); σ<sub>cr</sub> = N<sub>cr</sub>/t the critical stress (Pa); k the buckling coefficient (dimensionless); b the loaded edge width, across the load (m); r = a/b the aspect ratio; m the number of half-waves along the load, chosen to make k smallest.

blocks.text: Each m gives a curve of k against r with minimum 4 at r = m. The plate takes whichever m gives the lowest k. Curves m and m + 1 cross at r = √(m(m + 1)): 1.41, 2.45, 3.46. So the plate changes from one half-wave to two at a/b = 1.41. For a long plate k stays between 4 and 4.5 and tends to 4: the plate buckles into nearly square half-waves about b long, and N<sub>cr</sub> ≈ 4π²D/b², independent of length.
Other edge supports change k. For long plates in uniform compression, with the loaded ends simply supported, the usual values are:

head: Unloaded long edges
k (long plate)
Where it applies
rows: skin between stringers, a web between flanges
skin next to a stiff spar cap
upper bound for skin riveted to stiff stringers

blocks.text: Real riveted skins lie between the simply supported and clamped values; designers usually take k = 4 because it is safe. A free edge drops k almost tenfold, which is why outstanding flanges have small b/t limits. Because σ<sub>cr</sub> depends on (t/b)², halving the stringer pitch raises the buckling stress four times, and doubling the skin thickness does the same.

Buckling is not collapse. At N<sub>cr</sub> a small deflection grows without extra load, but a plate supported on all its edges then develops membrane tension across the buckles and carries more load, until the stringers fail or the material yields. If σ<sub>cr</sub> exceeds the proportional limit, E in the formula is replaced by a reduced (tangent) modulus, and the elastic answer is too high.

figure.caption: Buckling coefficient k against aspect ratio for a plate simply supported on all edges in uniaxial compression. Each dashed curve is one number of half-waves m; the plate follows the lowest (solid line), changing mode at a/b = 1.41 and 2.45. The first worked example (a/b = 2) sits on a minimum, k = 4.00 with m = 2; the second (a/b = 1.5) has k = 4.34.

examples.question: A rectangular plate with a = 1.2 m along the load and b = 0.6 m across it is simply supported on all edges. It is 3 mm thick, with E = 70 GPa and ν = 0.30, and is compressed along x. Find D, the buckling coefficient and mode, the critical load per unit width and the critical stress.
steps: k = (m/r + r/m)²: m = 1 gives (0.5 + 2)² = 6.25; m = 2 gives (1 + 1)² = 4.00; m = 3 gives (1.5 + 0.667)² = 4.69. The lowest is k = 4.00 with m = 2: two half-waves, each 0.6 m long.
Check by the stress form: 4π² × 70 × 10⁹/(12 × 0.91) × (0.003/0.6)² = 6.33 MPa.
examples.answer: D = 173.1 N·m; k = 4.00 with m = 2; N<sub>cr</sub> = 18.98 kN/m; σ<sub>cr</sub> = 6.33 MPa.

examples.question: A wing skin panel between two stringers and two ribs is 450 mm long (along the load) and 300 mm wide, 2 mm thick, with E = 72 GPa and ν = 0.33. Take all edges simply supported. Find k, the mode and σ<sub>cr</sub>. Compare with the long-plate value, and with a stringer flange of the same width and thickness that has one free edge.
steps: r = 450/300 = 1.5, between the crossing points 1.41 and 2.45, so m = 2 should control.
Long-plate value with k = 4: 11.8 N/mm², 8% lower; the short panel gains a little from its ribs.
Flange with one free edge, k = 0.425: σ<sub>cr</sub> = 1.26 N/mm², about a tenth of the skin value. A flange of this width would be useless; flanges are made much narrower.
examples.answer: k = 4.34 with two half-waves; σ<sub>cr</sub> = 12.8 N/mm² (long-plate 11.8, free-edge flange 1.26 N/mm²).

traps: Using Euler's column formula for a plate. A plate supported along its sides buckles at a load set by its width b and k, not by its length.
Putting a instead of b in N<sub>cr</sub> = kπ²D/b². b is the loaded edge, across the load; a enters only through k.
Assuming k = 4 for every plate. It is 4 only at whole-number aspect ratios or for long plates with both unloaded edges simply supported; a free edge gives 0.425.
Mixing sign conventions. The buckling equation here takes compression positive; the general plate equation takes tension positive.
Reporting N<sub>cr</sub> in N/m as a stress. Divide by t for σ<sub>cr</sub>.

quiz.q: Write the governing equation for plate buckling and state the sign convention used.
quiz.a: D∇⁴w + N<sub>x</sub> ∂²w/∂x² + 2N<sub>xy</sub> ∂²w/∂x∂y + N<sub>y</sub> ∂²w/∂y² = 0, with N<sub>x</sub>, N<sub>y</sub>, N<sub>xy</sub> positive in compression.

quiz.q: What do m and n mean in w = A sin(mπx/a) sin(nπy/b)?
quiz.a: m is the number of half sine waves along the load (x), n the number across (y); A is the small, undetermined amplitude.

quiz.q: Why does a long simply supported plate buckle at a load almost independent of its length?
quiz.a: It chooses m so that each half-wave is close to b long, which keeps k near its minimum of 4. N<sub>cr</sub> ≈ 4π²D/b² then depends on b and D only.

quiz.q: For a simply supported plate with a/b = 3, compute k for m = 2, 3 and 4 and state the controlling mode.
A simply supported plate has b = 0.5 m and D = 200 N·m. Take k = 4. Find N<sub>cr</sub>.
A designer halves the stringer pitch, keeping the skin thickness. What happens to N<sub>cr</sub> and σ<sub>cr</sub>, and why might this not halve the panel weight saving?
quiz.a: Both rise four times, since they vary as 1/b². But twice as many stringers are needed, so the weight saved in skin is partly spent on stringers; the best pitch balances the two.

quiz.q: Explain why buckling of a skin panel at σ<sub>cr</sub> is not failure of the panel.
quiz.a: σ<sub>cr</sub> is a bifurcation: the flat shape stops being the only equilibrium. The panel is held on all four sides, so as it buckles membrane tension develops across the buckles and the stiff edges near the stringers keep carrying more load. Failure comes later, when the stringers cripple or the material yields.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real panels have initial waviness, so they bend gradually instead of bifurcating, and post-buckling is followed with the large-deflection von Kármán equations. Curved panels and cylinders buckle very differently and need knock-down factors from tests. Search for Rayleigh–Ritz plate buckling and NASA SP-8007.
